questions.q: How does Foer describe modern animal agriculture?
a: As factories that produce meat as fast and cheaply as possible
As small farms that treat animals with care and respect
As a traditional practice that has barely changed
As a regulated industry focused on animal welfare
questions.why: Lesson 1 says raising animals has become producing them in factories, where speed and low cost matter more than wellbeing.

questions.q: What is the fecal soup used in poultry processing?
a: A broth of dead chickens and waste that adds weight to meat
A cleaning solution used to kill bacteria on the factory floor
A feed mixture given to chickens to speed their growth
A natural fertilizer sprayed on fields near the farms
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes chicken meat being immersed in a broth of dead chickens containing feces and pathogens to absorb extra weight.

questions.q: What share of store chicken carried salmonella or campylobacter?
a: 83 percent
33 percent
18 percent
50 percent
questions.why: Lesson 2 cites a consumer report finding that 83 percent of chicken meat in stores contained salmonella or campylobacter.

questions.q: Why is routine antibiotic use on farms a health threat?
a: It breeds resistant germs that can move from animals to people
It makes meat lose most of its protein and vitamins
It causes chickens to grow too slowly to be profitable
It makes animal waste more toxic than human sewage
questions.why: Lesson 2 says overusing antibiotics, often preventively, creates resistant pathogens that can pass from animals to humans.

questions.q: How do livestock emissions compare with the world's transport emissions?
a: They are 40 percent higher, about 18 percent of the total
They are 40 percent lower, about 5 percent of the total
They are roughly equal at about 18 percent each
They are twice as high, about 40 percent of the total
questions.why: Lesson 3 says animal agriculture produces 40 percent more greenhouse gases than transport, accounting for up to 18 percent of global emissions.
